summary: Describes the SIP PUBLISH extension for publishing event state used within the SIP Events framework. Its first use is publishing presence information, but it can support other kinds of event state too.

plainLanguage.summary: SIP PUBLISH lets an endpoint send event information, such as presence, to a server. The server tracks each publication and can combine information from several endpoints for subscribers.

questions: how does sip presence publication work
what is an event state compositor
subtitle: SIP PUBLISH sends event state to a server that combines it and shares it with subscribers.

tldr.problem: The SIP Events framework supports subscriptions to event state, but user agents needed a standard way to publish their own state to the server that distributes it.
tldr.mechanism: PUBLISH sends event state to an Event State Compositor. The server returns an entity-tag, which the publisher uses to refresh, replace, or remove that publication before it expires.
tldr.outcome: The mechanism supports presence and other event packages. RFC 3903 is a Proposed Standard updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 3903 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2004. It has been updated by RFC 8996 and has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Publishing Event State
sections.content:
RFC 3903 adds the PUBLISH method to the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP). It lets a user agent send event state to a server that combines the state and distributes it through the SIP Events framework. The first defined use is presence.

The mechanism can support other event packages that define suitable state. It is not intended as a general way to transport arbitrary data. Several user agents may publish different parts of one resource's state.
sections.plainLanguage: PUBLISH gives a user agent a standard way to send event information to a server. Presence is one use, and other event packages can define their own state format.

sections.title: Publishers, Compositors, and Expiring State
sections.content:
An Event Publication Agent (EPA) is the client that sends PUBLISH requests. An Event State Compositor (ESC) is the server that processes them and combines state for a resource. For presence, these roles correspond to a presence user agent and a presence agent.

PUBLISHED event state is soft state: it has a lifetime and expires unless refreshed. The ESC assigns an entity-tag to identify each successful publication. The RFC also recognizes hard state, a default state maintained by the ESC, but defining how to set or combine it is outside the document's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: A publisher sends its own state, and a compositor combines state for others to receive. Each publication expires unless its publisher refreshes it.

sections.title: How a Publication Is Identified
sections.content:
A publication is identified by its Request-URI, its Event header, and, when updating existing state, an entity-tag. The Request-URI names the resource. The Event header names the event package. A successful PUBLISH response always returns a SIP-ETag value that the EPA stores.

To refresh, modify, or remove a publication, the EPA sends its tag in SIP-If-Match. Tags are opaque identifiers; the client must not infer meaning from their format. An expired or removed tag is invalid, so the EPA starts a new initial publication if it needs to publish again.
sections.plainLanguage: The resource address and Event header identify what state is being published. The server's tag identifies one publication and must be returned when that publication changes.

sections.title: Four PUBLISH Operations
sections.content:
The request body, SIP-If-Match header, and Expires value determine the operation. An initial publication has a body and no SIP-If-Match. A refresh has a tag but no body. A modification has both a tag and a body. A removal has a tag, no body, and Expires set to zero.

The ESC may shorten the requested expiration but cannot extend it. Its successful response states the actual lifetime and supplies a new SIP-ETag. A 412 response means the tag did not match; the EPA must discard it and must not retry that request. It should begin with an initial publication instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A PUBLISH request can create, renew, change, or remove one publication. The body and tag distinguish these operations, and Expires tells the server how long the state should last.

sections.title: How the Server Processes Requests
sections.content:
The ESC processes requests for the same Request-URI in arrival order and atomically: a request completes fully or does not take effect. It checks that it manages the resource, supports the Event package, and can match any supplied tag. It then checks the content type and expiration interval before storing, refreshing, or removing state.

The server returns an error for an unknown resource, unsupported event, unmatched tag, unsupported content type, or too-short expiration interval. A successful response is 200 OK with the chosen Expires value and a new SIP-ETag. OPTIONS can advertise PUBLISH and supported event packages.
sections.plainLanguage: The server checks the resource, event type, tag, body, and expiration before changing state. It either completes the whole request or returns an error without applying it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Event state may be sensitive. The ESC should authenticate publishers, apply authorization rules, and throttle publications and resulting notifications to limit resource exhaustion. Both ESCs and EPAs must support Digest authentication with replay protection.

A person between the publisher and server could alter or remove state. The RFC requires ESCs to implement TLS with one-way and mutual authentication and the SIPS URI scheme. It recommends integrity protection for key headers and the request body. Implementations may also use S/MIME for integrity or confidentiality.
sections.plainLanguage: Event state can reveal private information, so the server should check who may publish it. Secure connections and replay protection help prevent others from changing or repeating publications.

sections.title: Registered SIP Elements
sections.content: The RFC registers the PUBLISH method, response code 412 (Conditional Request Failed), and the SIP-ETag and SIP-If-Match header names. Neither new header has a compact form. The RFC's examples show how a publisher sends state, receives a tag, refreshes it, and sends a modification that can notify subscribers.
sections.plainLanguage: The method, response code, and two header names are registered so SIP implementations can recognize the publication exchange consistently.
